ideas.title: Effective-bets throttle with a daily turnover budget
ideas.sketch: Each close, build the 10x10 correlation matrix of daily log returns over a 63-day and a 21-day window, take its eigenvalues (they sum to 10), and compute the entropy effective number of bets N_eff = exp(-sum p_i ln p_i) with p_i = lambda_i/10, so N_eff runs from 1 (one factor) to 10 (independent). Divide each window's N_eff by its own trailing 756-day median (expanding after a 126-day minimum; the ratio cancels small-sample bias, which is worst at 21 days) and set total exposure s = clip(min(ratio_63, ratio_21), 0.25, 1); the fast window cuts risk early, the slow one delays re-entry. Target weights are s times inverse-volatility (63-day) weights, each capped at 20% of the sleeve with the excess redistributed pro rata; the remainder 1-s is cash, and s is the only use of correlation, so no return forecast is needed. Signals are computed at close t and traded at close t+1. Constraints hold by construction: every day one-way traded value is capped at 3.5% of NAV (5 x 3.5% = 17.5% per week, under 20% even if cash counts as a position), with priority to (i) sells that lower exposure, (ii) inverse-vol rebalancing, (iii) buys that raise exposure, scaled pro rata when the budget binds. There is no deadband, so any nonzero gap is traded on each of 5 days (at least 3 in every week). Rationale: the 20% drawdown bound is broken by correlated sell-offs (2008 risk-asset block, March 2020 liquidation, 2022 stock-bond correlation turning positive), each of which collapses N_eff before or during the loss. Honest estimate: the unthrottled inverse-vol book has about 6% volatility and roughly -16% in 2022, and the throttle should bring that to about -10% to -14%; the 17.5% weekly speed limit is the main residual risk in a one-week crash. Expected net growth is about 4-5% per year, from harvesting equity, credit, term, inflation and commodity premia at low risk, with cost drag under 0.3% per year at 3 bp per unit traded.

ideas.title: Down-day correlation gap ladder on Mon/Wed/Fri
ideas.sketch: The signal is the loss of diversification precisely on down days, following the known asymmetry that correlations rise when markets fall. Let m_t be the equal-weight mean of the 10 daily returns; over the trailing 126 days split days into down (m<0) and up (m>=0), and compute the average pairwise correlation of the 10 assets on each subset, rho_D and rho_U (about 55-70 observations each, standard error near 0.13, which is why 126 rather than 63 days). Set exposure E = clip(1 - (rho_D - rho_U)/(1 - rho_U), 0.25, 1), the fraction of the diversification headroom above the benign-state correlation that is lost in stress: E = 1 when down-day and up-day structure match, and E falls toward the 0.25 floor as rho_D approaches 1. Target weights are E times inverse-volatility (63-day) weights capped at 20% per ETF (excess redistributed pro rata to uncapped names), with 1-E in cash. Trades occur only on the first, the ceil((n+1)/2)-th and the last trading day of each week (n trading days: Mon/Wed/Fri in a full week), each capped at 6% of NAV one-way, which gives at least 3 trade days and at most 18% weekly turnover by construction, while ordering trades as de-risking sells first, then rebalancing, then buys; signals use the previous close and execute at the next trade-day close. Only three parameters exist (126-day window, 0.25 floor, 6% clip) and each has a stated principle: statistical precision of the correlation estimate, a floor that keeps the book diversified and invested, and a 20% budget divided over three days. The signal is meant to fire in equity-bond regimes such as 2022 (down-day correlation between stocks, bonds and credit jumps while up-day correlation stays low) and in 2008 and 2020; it lags a one-week crash, so the worst case is estimated at -11% to -15% for a book with about 6% base volatility, not proven below 20%.
